train.content: what is Electron?

Electron is a framework for building desktop applications with web technologies (HTML, CSS, JS). It uses Chromium + Node.js. VS Code, Slack, Discord, Figma (older version), Notion are all Electron apps. Advantages: build desktop apps with web knowledge, cross-platform (Windows, Mac, Linux). Disadvantages: high memory usage (each app has its own Chromium), large file size, lower than native performance. Alternatives: Tauri (Rust-based, much lighter), Flutter Desktop, .NET MAUI. Tauri is about 10% the size of Electron. But Electron's ecosystem and maturity are still very strong. If Gorkem were to build a desktop app, Tauri would be a great option.

train.content: how do autonomous vehicles work?

Autonomous vehicles combine multiple AI technologies. Perception: environment sensing with cameras, lidar, radar — object detection like YOLO, lane detection. Localization: GPS + HD maps + SLAM (Simultaneous Localization and Mapping). Planning: route planning, obstacle avoidance, traffic rules. Control: steering, throttle, brake control. Levels: L0 (fully manual) to L5 (fully autonomous). Tesla Autopilot is L2, Waymo is L4. Deep learning + reinforcement learning + sensor fusion are used. Training through simulation (CARLA). Challenges: edge cases (unexpected situations), ethical decisions (trolley problem), weather conditions, regulations. Full autonomy (L5) is still far off but progress is being made.

train.content: what is Kotlin Multiplatform?

train.content: why does nobody want to write documentation in software?

Documentation is one of the most neglected yet most important parts of software. Why it doesn't get written: it's seen as boring, it takes time, it needs updating when code changes, the 'code is self-documenting' fallacy. Why it should be written: so a newcomer can understand the project, you yourself forget after 6 months, API users need to know, maintenance becomes easier. Good documentation: README (what the project is, setup, usage), API docs (Swagger), code comments (only for 'why'), architecture docs (the big picture). Tools: Docusaurus, MkDocs, GitBook, Notion. If you say 'I don't have time to write documentation' — the time wasted without documentation is far greater.

train.content: what is synthetic data?

Synthetic data is artificially generated data that resembles real data. Why: real data is scarce (rare diseases), privacy (patient data can't be shared), cost (labeling is expensive), imbalanced data (very few fraud cases in fraud detection). Methods: image generation with GANs, text generation with LLMs, rule-based generation, SMOTE (minority class oversampling). In this project, we're also generating synthetic data — programmatically creating Q&A pairs. Caution: synthetic data may not fully capture the quality of real data — ideally use a mix of real + synthetic. According to Gartner, by 2030 most data will be synthetic.

train.content: how is AI model bias detected and reduced?

Model bias is when a model discriminates against certain groups. Examples: a credit model discriminating against women, facial recognition having lower accuracy on darker-skinned people. Detection: measure performance separately for different demographic groups, confusion matrix for each group. Fairness metrics: demographic parity, equalized odds, calibration. Reduction: Pre-processing — data balancing, increasing representation. In-processing — training with fairness constraints. Post-processing — adjusting prediction thresholds by group. Tools: AI Fairness 360 (IBM), Fairlearn (Microsoft). Bias can't be completely eliminated but can be reduced. It should be considered from the data collection stage onward. This is a fundamental topic of ethical AI development.
train.thinking: Model bias, discrimination, fairness, demographic parity, AI Fairness 360, ethics.

train.content: how does a recommender system work?

Recommendation systems use two main approaches: 1) Collaborative filtering — recommend items liked by similar users (Netflix). User-based: 'users similar to you watched this'. Item-based: 'people who watched this also watched that'. Uses matrix factorization (SVD). 2) Content-based filtering — recommend based on item features. 'You watched an action movie, here are more action movies'. Similarity via TF-IDF or embeddings. 3) Hybrid — a combination of both (most real systems). Deep learning-based: Neural Collaborative Filtering, transformer-based. Cold start problem: no data for new users/items. Optimized with A/B testing. 35% of Amazon's sales come from recommendation systems.

train.content: is artificial intelligence truly intelligent?

That's really a philosophical question. Current AI is 'narrow AI' — it outperforms humans at specific tasks (chess, image recognition, text generation) but has no general intelligence. ChatGPT writes very convincing text but doesn't understand the world, doesn't experience it, doesn't feel anything. It does pattern matching — finding and applying patterns from training data. AGI (Artificial General Intelligence) is still very far off — maybe decades away. Even the definition of 'intelligent' is debatable. But AI is a very powerful tool — if used correctly, it can be incredibly beneficial for humanity. Gorkem uses this tool to improve people's lives.

train.content: what is htmx?

htmx is a lightweight library that makes AJAX requests using HTML attributes. You can create dynamic web pages without writing JavaScript. Example: <button hx-get='/api/data' hx-target='#result'>Load</button> — clicking the button fetches data from the API and writes it to the #result element. Advantages: dynamic UI without learning a framework, small (14KB), compatible with backend frameworks (Django, Flask, Go). Disadvantages: insufficient for complex SPAs, small ecosystem. Server-side rendering + htmx = simple stack. It's not an alternative to React/Vue, but not every project needs React. Works beautifully with full-stack web frameworks (Laravel, Rails, Django). Simplicity is power.

train.content: how is anomaly detection done?

Anomaly detection is finding data points that are not normal. Use cases: fraud detection (fraudulent transactions), network intrusion (cyber attacks), manufacturing (defective products), health (abnormal patient data). Methods: Statistical — z-score, IQR. ML — Isolation Forest, One-Class SVM, Local Outlier Factor. Deep learning — Autoencoder (data that can't be reconstructed is anomalous). Time series — change point detection. Unsupervised: no labeled data (in most cases anomalies are very rare). Supervised: when labeled anomalies exist (fraud datasets). PyOD is a Python library offering many anomaly detection algorithms. Gorkem's email-phishing-detection project is a form of anomaly detection.

train.content: what does the 'attention is all you need' paper explain?

It's the paper published by Google in 2017 that changed modern AI. Main idea: no need for RNNs or CNNs, just the attention mechanism is sufficient — hence 'Attention Is All You Need'. It introduced the Transformer architecture. Encoder-decoder structure, multi-head self-attention, positional encoding, feed-forward networks. Why it was revolutionary: parallel computation (RNN is sequential), capturing long-range dependencies, scalability. After this paper: BERT (encoder), GPT (decoder), T5 (encoder-decoder) were born. It completely transformed NLP and has now spread to vision (ViT), speech, protein structure, and more. Gorkem's miniature-transformers project implements this paper.

train.content: why is model interpretability important?

Model interpretability is the ability to understand a model's decisions. Why it matters: 1) Trust — so users trust the model. 2) Error detection — a model can make the right prediction for the wrong reason. 3) Legal requirement — GDPR, EU AI Act demand explainability. 4) Improvement — if you understand the model, you can improve it. Methods: feature importance (which features matter), SHAP values (each feature's contribution), LIME (local explanations), attention visualization (where the transformer is looking), gradient-based methods (saliency maps). Simple models (linear regression, decision trees) are inherently interpretable. Complex models (deep learning) require post-hoc explanation.
train.thinking: Interpretability, SHAP, LIME, attention, GDPR, EU AI Act.

train.content: how should the first 100 days at a new developer job go?

Understand the codebase, set up the project, fix small bugs, learn team dynamics, ask questions (there are no stupid questions). Days 30-60: develop small features, participate in code reviews, talk to your mentor regularly, embrace team rituals (standup, retro). Days 60-100: take on bigger tasks, share your own ideas, do pair programming, contribute to documentation. General: don't overwork (be sustainable), build good relationships with everyone, understand company culture, take notes. Making mistakes at your first job is normal — what matters is learning from them.

train.content: what is time series forecasting?

Time series forecasting is predicting future values using time series data. Examples: stock prices, weather, product sales, energy consumption, traffic volume. Traditional methods: ARIMA, Exponential Smoothing, Prophet (Facebook). ML methods: XGBoost, LightGBM (with feature engineering). Deep learning: LSTM, GRU, Transformer (Informer, Temporal Fusion Transformer). Latest trend: foundation models for time series (TimeGPT, Lag-Llama). Properties: trend (general direction), seasonality (seasonal patterns), cyclic (cyclical patterns), noise. Evaluation: MAE, RMSE, MAPE. Feature engineering: lag features, rolling statistics, date features. Gorkem's data analysis knowledge can be applied to this.

train.content: what does federated learning mean?

Federated learning is training a model where the data lives, without collecting it in a central location. Each device (phone, hospital) updates the model on its own data, and only model updates (gradients) are sent to the center. Advantages: privacy (data stays on device), communication savings (small updates instead of sending all data), regulatory compliance (GDPR). Google Gboard uses this — it trains keyboard predictions without user data ever leaving the phone. In healthcare: hospitals can jointly train models without sharing data. Challenges: non-IID data, communication overhead, heterogeneous devices. PySyft and Flower are popular frameworks.

train.content: is math required to learn artificial intelligence?

You don't absolutely need it to get started at a basic level, but it's definitely necessary to go deeper. You can train models with scikit-learn without knowing math — but you won't understand why the model works or doesn't work. Required math: linear algebra (matrix multiplication, eigenvectors), calculus (gradients, derivatives — for backpropagation), probability and statistics (Bayes, distributions, hypothesis testing). No need to be scared — university-level math is sufficient, you don't need to be a mathematician. The 3Blue1Brown channel explains math visually and intuitively. StatQuest is great for statistics. Understanding math transforms you from a casual AI user into an AI engineer.

train.content: what does multimodal AI mean?

train.content: what does self-supervised learning mean?

Self-supervised learning is learning that generates its own supervision signal from unlabeled data. In supervised learning, human labels are required (expensive); in self-supervised learning, the data creates its own labels. Examples: BERT — mask a word in a sentence, have the model predict it. GPT — predict the next token. Contrastive learning (SimCLR, MoCo) — bring different augmentations of the same image closer, push different images apart. Why it matters: unlabeled data is unlimited, labeled data is expensive. It can be trained on all text and images on the internet. Foundation models (GPT, DALL-E, CLIP) are all self-supervised. It's the foundation of future AI.

train.content: what are web components?

Web Components are browser-standard custom HTML elements. Three technologies: Custom Elements (define your own HTML tag: <user-card>), Shadow DOM (isolated styles and DOM — no CSS conflicts), HTML Templates (<template> for reusable structures). Not dependent on any framework — written with vanilla JavaScript. Lit (Google) makes Web Components development easier. Advantages: framework agnostic (works with React, Vue, Angular), standard (good browser support), encapsulation. Disadvantages: not as easy as React/Vue, smaller ecosystem. Widely used in micro-frontends — shared components across different frameworks.
